sections.content: The *imperfecto* sets the scene: what was going on, what things were like, what used to happen. The *indefinido* is the event that interrupts the scene or moves the story on. A common pattern is *mientras* + *imperfecto*, followed by an *indefinido*.

sections.title: Which tense?
rows: llovía, hacía frío, la gente esperaba
imperfecto: the scene, something in progress
de niño solía leer; cada verano íbamos al mar
imperfecto: habits, what used to happen
llegó el autobús, empezó a llover
indefinido: a finished event that moves the story on

items.spanish: Mientras esperábamos el autobús, empezó a llover.
items.english: While we were waiting for the bus, it started to rain.

items.spanish: Hacía frío y la calle estaba vacía.
items.english: It was cold and the street was empty.

items.spanish: De niño, solía caminar a la escuela con mi hermano.
items.english: As a child, I used to walk to school with my brother.

items.spanish: Estábamos charlando cuando sonó el teléfono.
items.english: We were chatting when the phone rang.

sections.content: Ask whether the verb is the stage or the action on it. The stage (weather, time, feelings, what was in progress) takes the *imperfecto*; the action takes the *indefinido*. For past habits, *soler* is used in the *imperfecto*: *solía*, *solíamos*.

sections.topic: the imperfect tense for past habits and descriptions
